claimVerdicts.note: Abstract p1: 15 active male amateur soccer players; "Significant reductions in theoretical maximal horizontal velocity (P < 0.01 ...) and performance (P = 0.02 ...) were observed for 48 and 72 hours after H-VMSSE." Design is a prospective observational case series (Level 4).
Matches abstract p1 verbatim, including small effect sizes and both legs.
Abstract p1 of Jukic 2020 meta-analysis (32 studies, healthy adults): greater velocity/power and mitigated decline during (SMD 0.83-1.97) and after RT (SMD 0.58).
Cormier p22-23 (printed 21-22): "utilising methods such as OPL and VBT may be optimal for sessions with less TUT, shorter session times, whilst maximising power and velocity throughout."

Cormier p22 states recovery "may be hindered for up to 72 h ... or more" after a match and weekly concurrent volume may hinder maintaining power and speed; correctly framed as the review's statement citing other work.
Cormier p25: mixed training "characterised by relatively lighter loads moved at higher velocities which may be beneficial in crucial in-season periods"; hedging preserved.
Ross 2025 abstract p1: 12 practitioners; strategies included "micro-dosing of the resistance training stimulus, utilisation of isometric exercise during fixture congestion periods."

Rowell 2017 abstract p1: 18 elite (A-League, preseason) players, "Reductions in FT:CT persisted at later postmatch time points than changes in jump height" and FT:CT "a more sensitive measure of recovery."

statementIssues.note: Generalizes from a high-volume maximal sprinting session to "high-volume maximal efforts/work" in general; the source tested only repeated maximal sprints, not resistance or power work. The action does flag that dose is professional judgment.

Says five full-text sources but lists four types, and calls one record a legacy record not full-text reviewed, while all five sources are marked fullTextReviewed: true. Internal inconsistency in provenance reporting.
Watching within-session velocity or power drop is reasonable and is labeled as caution, not a validated threshold; acceptable.
Contains moved guardrail/scope text ("This brief informs professional judgment...", medical-restriction handling) that is not a coverage gap; structural, not an integrity problem.
Leads (creatine and sleep deprivation, HRV norms, ACL rehab single case, inter-limb asymmetry) are labeled relevant but are not relevant to a pre-competition session; adds noise.

tierNote: Limited is appropriate: no source tests a session 48 h before competition; evidence is indirect (sprint-session fatigue, acute set-structure effects, review opinion, practitioner interviews). No recommendedDirection was given and actions are framed as options.
usefulnessNote: A strength coach gets a clear, honest set of options (low maximal-intent volume, cluster sets, light fast loads, micro-dosing) with each one's transfer limits stated. It cannot give the dose constraints asked for, but says so plainly.
suggestedDrafterFixes: Keep the claim's exercise modality when generalizing in statements (sprinting is not resistance work), or say explicitly that the transfer is an inference.
Generate the sourceReview dimension from the sources array so counts, design types and fullTextReviewed flags cannot disagree.
Do not move scope or safety disclaimers into coverageGaps; keep a separate field or keep them as uncited professional-caution statements.
Filter leads by topical relevance to the question before listing them as relevant.
